issues.legal_issue: A tenant or the tenant’s successors cannot be evicted solely for acquiring residential accommodation when the rented premises were let for both residence and professional or business use.
material_facts: The premises were let to a practising lawyer for residence, and the landlord gave written consent for a professional office to be maintained there along with the residence.
The courts below found that the premises had been let for, and used for, both residence and professional purposes; that concurrent finding was accepted as final.
After the original tenant died, his successors continued to live in the premises, and two of them later used it for professional offices.
The successors had built a residential house, and eviction was sought on the ground that they had acquired residential accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The successors could not be evicted solely because they had acquired residential accommodation, since the tenancy was for the composite purpose of residence and professional use.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 13(1)(h) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and section 14(1)(h) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, acquisition of residential accommodation does not justify eviction where the rented premises were let for both residence and professional or business use. The definition of premises in section 2(g) of the 1952 Act and section 2(1) of the 1958 Act accommodates combined uses. The Court applied Dr. Gopal Das Verma v. Dr. S. K. Bhardwaj, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 678, and held that a dominant-intention test did not govern the question. The same position applied to the tenant’s heirs and legal representatives.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.composite_residential_and_professional_l: The premises were let for both residence and professional or business use.
predicates.tenant_or_successors_acquired_residentia: The tenant or the tenant’s successors acquired residential accommodation.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding concerns premises let for both residential and professional or business use, acquiring residential accommodation by the tenant or successors does not, by itself, permit eviction.

issues.legal_issue: Pending proceedings under a repealed rent-control law continue under that law, subject to applicable slight modifications or clarifications in the replacement law.
material_facts: The eviction suit began under the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952.
The Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 came into force while the suit was pending.
The replacement Act omitted the word “suitable” from the corresponding ground for eviction.
issues.conclusion: The pending proceeding ordinarily continued under the 1952 Act, while slight modifications or clarifications in the 1958 Act were to be applied; whether either Act governed, the result in this case was the same.
issues.legal_principle: Section 57(2) and its first proviso of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, preserve pending proceedings under the repealed Act while requiring regard to the replacement Act. Karam Singh Sobhi v. Shri Pratap Chand, [1964] 4 S.C.R. 647, and Brij Kishore v. Vishww Mitter Kapur, as cited in the judgment, establish that the old Act ordinarily governs pending proceedings, with slight modifications or clarifications in the new Act applying harmoniously with that rule.

predicates.replacement_law_makes_slight_modificatio: The replacement law makes a slight modification or clarification to the relevant prior provision.

issues.definition: A pending proceeding under a repealed rent-control law continues under that law, with any applicable slight modification or clarification in the replacement law.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord cannot recast professional use as a personal licence that ended on the original tenant’s death when the final factual finding is that the premises were let for both residence and professional use.
material_facts: The courts below concurrently found that the premises had been let to the original tenant for residence and professional or business use.
The landlord argued that the written permission for professional use was a personal licence that ended when the original tenant died.
The Court treated the concurrent finding about the purpose of the letting as final.
issues.conclusion: The argument that the permission was a personal licence ending on the original tenant’s death could not be entertained in view of the final finding that the premises had been let for composite use.
issues.legal_principle: Where a concurrent finding of fact establishes that premises were let for residence-cum-professional or business use, a submission that permission for the additional use was merely a personal licence ending on the tenant’s death cannot be entertained in the face of that finding.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.final_finding_of_composite_letting: The final factual finding is that the premises were let for both residence and professional or business use.
predicates.landlord_claims_professional_use_was_per: The landlord argues that permission for professional or business use was personal to the original tenant and ended on that tenant’s death.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, when the final finding establishes a composite letting, a landlord’s claim that the additional use was a personal permission ending at the tenant’s death is not entertained.
